Molecular imaging is defined as the in vivo visualization, characterization, and quantification of
biologic processes at the cellular and molecular level.1,2
Molecular imaging techniques include nuclear medicine, optical imaging, ultrasonography with
contrast, functional MRI, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy.3

Definition
Molecular imaging comprises the set of imaging studies that use patients’ physiology,
versus other imaging modalities, which only display anatomy. The techniques allow
orthopaedic surgeons to examine in vivo processes, such as metabolic activity, bone
turnover, and brain excitation. It offers advantages in diagnosis, staging, and
management of several orthopaedic diseases. The presence/absence of disease can be
evaluated in the absence of structural or anatomic changes.
Nuclear Medicine
Nuclear medicine involves the use of radioactive materials or radiopharmaceuticals for
diagnostic, therapeutic, and research purposes.4
A radiopharmaceutical is composed of a radioactive component bound to an organic
molecule. The organic molecule carries the radioactive component to specific tissues, organs,
or cells.
The radioactive component is detected by external devices for diagnostic imaging.
The radioactive component is absorbed if used for management.5

Nuclear Medicine
Nuclear medicine involves the administration of a radioactive agent to a patient
(radiopharmaceutical). That agent goes to a target tissue (eg, bone), and the radioactivity
related to that agent is recorded by a detector (such as a gamma ray camera, which is
similar to a panel of Geiger counters) placed over the body or a body part.
Radiopharmaceutical concentration within the body is termed uptake. The

radiopharmaceuticals most frequently used in orthopaedics are summarized in Table 1.
Certain radiopharmaceuticals emit gamma rays suitable for gamma cameras, which can
generate planar and single photon emission CT (SPECT) scans. Other
radiopharmaceuticals are positron-emitting and produce pairs of gamma rays detectable
via positron emission tomography (PET) cameras. SPECT and PET cameras often are
combined with low-dose CT, generating fused SPECT/CT or PET/CT images to better
localize areas of increased uptake. Low-dose CT scans provide less anatomical detail
than standard CT scans.
Radiopharmaceuticals that emit beta particles or alpha particles may be used for
therapeutic use, specifically the management of tumors.6

Bone Scintigraphy
Diagnostic nuclear imaging test used to evaluate active bone formation
The distribution of the radiopharmaceuticals used in bone scintigraphy depends on regional
blood flow and osteogenic activity.7,8 It is an extremely sensitive method for detecting
musculoskeletal pathologies of increased bone turnover/remodeling and for increased or
decreased vascularization. Common clinical indications are listed in Table 2.
Table 2 Common Clinical Indications for Bone Scintigraphy in Orthopaedics
Primary bone tumors
Metastatic osseous disease
Tumor-like conditions: Paget disease, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, fibrous dysplasia
Trauma: fractures, shin splints, enthesopathies
Heterotopic ossification/soft-tissue calcification
Musculoskeletal inflammation and infection
Orthopaedic hardware/prosthetic joint complications
Metabolic bone disease
Bone viability: grafts, infarcts, osteonecrosis
Complex regional pain syndrome

Bone Scintigraphy
Performed with technetium (Tc)-99m–labeled diphosphonates using a gamma camera or
with fluorine-18 sodium fluoride (18F-NaF) using PET/CT.
Tc-99m–Labeled Diphosphonate Bone Scintigraphy
Most common type of bone scintigraphy
The mechanism of bone uptake of these phosphate analogs is via chemisorption onto the
bone surface. They subsequently attach to hydroxyapatite crystals and become incorporated
into sites of active bone turnover.
Approximately 50% to 60% of diphosphonates localize in bone and the remainder is excreted
by the kidneys.9
The bone is the organ that receives the highest dose of radiation.10-13
Bone scintigraphy can be performed as a single-phase delayed or multiphase imaging.

Tc-99m–Labeled Diphosphonate Bone Scintigraphy
For single phase, imaging is performed 2 to 4 hours after radiopharmaceutical
intravenous injection. Planar anterior and posterior whole-body images of the entire
axial and appendicular skeleton are obtained. Supplementary localized or spot images
can be obtained (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Technetium-99m–methylene diphosphonate bone scans of a 72-year-old man
with back pain and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. Anterior (A) and posterior (B)
whole-body bone scans show abnormal activity in the lumbar spine (arrows) and the
right iliac bone (arrowheads). C, Posterior bone scan of the chest shows tracer activity
involving the anterior and posterior elements of L1 (arrow). This finding is known as the
Mickey Mouse sign, which is characteristic of Paget disease. (Courtesy of Juana Martinez,
MD, New York, NY.)
Three-phase (multiphase) bone scintigraphy consists of a first set of blood flow images
obtained during the radiopharmaceutical injection, a second set of blood pool/soft-
tissue images obtained 5 to 10 minutes after injection, and delayed/skeletal images
obtained 2 to 4 hours after radiopharmaceutical administration (Figure 2). If necessary,
additional delayed images can be obtained as long as 24 hours after injection to improve
skeletal detail in patients with impaired renal clearance. Common indications for
multiphase bone scintigraphy include infection, complex regional pain syndrome,
trauma, heterotopic ossification, and neoplasms.10,14-16 Multiphase bone scans are
commonly used to distinguish cellulitis (uptake only on first two phases) from
osteomyelitis (uptake on all three phases). If uptake is present in only the delayed bone
phase, surgeons should consider shin splints, stress fractures, and osteoblastic
metastasis.

SPECT acquires images via multiple views of the patient, resulting in three-dimensional
(3D) functional information. These 3D images are more detailed and include higher
contrast than planar images.17 The addition of SPECT scans to conventional planar bone
scans may increase sensitivity because of the better contrast resolution of 3D images
and may increase specificity because of the ability for better anatomic and morphologic
evaluation (eg, posterior elements of the spine). The combination of CT and SPECT may
further increase the specificity of the imaging modality, improving localization and

Gallium-67 Citrate Scintigraphy
Diagnostic nuclear imaging is primarily used in the evaluation of inflammation and infection.
Gallium (Ga)-67 emits a spectrum of gamma rays.
The mechanism of uptake of Ga-67 citrate in inflammatory sites is via different mechanisms.
After intravenous injection, in plasma Ga-67 binds to transferrin and is transported to affected
sites. It also binds to neutrophils, macrophages, and bacteria.
Radiopharmaceutical binds at the site of inflammation by 12 to 24 hours. In the first 24 hours
the primarily route of excretion is the kidneys. Subsequently, the principal route is
gastrointestinal. Normal distribution is observed in the bone marrow, liver, and spleen.
Imaging usually is performed 18 to 24 hours after radiopharmaceutical administration.
Anterior and posterior whole-body scans are obtained. Additional imaging via SPECT or
SPECT/CT for additional characterization of suspected sites may be useful.
Common clinical indications for Ga-67 citrate scintigraphy in orthopaedics are listed in Table
3.23,24 Ga-67 also accumulates in neoplasms and has been used in oncology for the evaluation
of lymphoma, lung, and other cancers.25
Table 3 Common Clinical Indications for Gallium-67 Citrate Scintigraphy in Orthopaedics
Osteomyelitis
Tuberculosis
Fungal infections
Chronic infections

The clinical utility of Ga-67 citrate scintigraphy is limited by the low specificity of the
study, delay in image acquisition, limited spatial resolution, and high radiation received
by the patient; therefore, it has been largely replaced by other imaging modalities with
more favorable properties. Currently, Ga-67 citrate scintigraphy is mainly indicated in the
evaluation of spinal infection, for which radiolabeled leukocyte scintigraphy has not
shown to be useful.26
Ga-67 citrate scintigraphy can be performed in combination with bone scintigraphy to
increase the specificity of the study in the diagnosis of infection, (Figure 4); however, the
addition of SPECT or SPECT/CT to Ga-67 citrate scintigraphy may avoid this dual
radiopharmaceutical imaging but still allow for the precise localization of uptake and
identification of soft-tissue involvement.27

aneurysm repair who has back pain, fever, and an elevated white blood cell count. A,

Radiolabeled Leukocyte Scintigraphy
Leukocytes can be labeled in vitro with indium (In)-111 oxyquinolone or Tc-99m exametazime
(Tc-99m hexamethylpropyleneamine oxime).
Most of the radiolabeled leukocytes are neutrophils, which are attracted to inflammation sites.
Blood is drawn from a patient, and the white cells are separated out, labeled, and re-injected.
Useful in the evaluation of different orthopaedic infections and inflammatory pathologies.
Common clinical indications are listed in Table 4.24,28
Table 4
Common Clinical Indications for Radiolabeled Leukocyte Scintigraphy in
Orthopaedics
Osteomyelitis
Orthopaedic hardware infections
Prosthetic joint infections
Postoperative infections
Diabetic foot infections
Neuropathic joint infections
Arthritis
Differentiation of infection from neoplasm

In-111 Oxyquinolone–Labeled Leukocyte Scintigraphy
Normal distribution to liver, spleen, and bone marrow
The radiolabeled leukocytes are administered intravenously.
The physical half-life of In-111 is 67 hours, allowing for delayed imaging, which is useful for
musculoskeletal pathologies. Whole-body planar images usually are obtained 18 to 24 hours
after injection (Figure 5). Pertinent SPECT of suspected sites of pathology also can be
performed.29
Figure 5 Images of the pelvis and lower extremities of a 19-year-old man with history of recent
osteosarcoma resection of the left femur in whom an infection was suspected. A, Indium-111
oxyquinolone–labeled leukocyte scan shows foci of increased activity in the distal femur, knee

Tc-99m Exametazime–Labeled Leukocyte Scintigraphy
The blood clearance half-life of Tc-99 hexamethylpropyleneamine–labeled leukocytes is 4
hours.
Imaging for musculoskeletal diseases is performed 4 to 8 hours after administration (Figure 6).
If the scan is negative or equivocal, delayed imaging may be performed 16 to 24 hours after
administration. Whole-body scans usually are obtained. A limited study or SPECT of the site of
interest may be performed in selected patients.

Tc-99m Exametazime-Labeled Leukocyte Scintigraphy
Advantages of Tc-99m hexamethylpropyleneamine–labeled leukocyte scintigraphy over
In-111 oxyquinolone–labeled leukocyte scintigraphy are lower radiation dose to the
patient, allowing for greater administered activity and resulting in higher resolution
images and earlier acquisition of imaging studies.
Disadvantages of this molecular imaging technique include the short half-life of the
radiopharmaceutical if delayed imaging is necessary. In addition, if bone marrow
scintigraphy is required, it cannot be performed simultaneously, and the time to obtain
results is prolonged.30
Bone Marrow Scintigraphy
Mainly performed in combination with radiolabeled leukocyte scintigraphy for the evaluation
of osteomyelitis
Commonly performed with Tc-99m sulfur colloid
The mechanism of uptake in the bone marrow is because of phagocytosis by
reticuloendothelial cells. It also is taken up by the reticuloendothelial cells in the spleen and by
Kupffer cells in the liver.
Imaging of the region of interest is performed 20 to 30 minutes after intravenous
administration.

Bone Marrow Scintigraphy
Bone marrow scintigraphy and In-111 oxyquinolone–labeled leukocyte scintigraphy can
be performed simultaneously as dual isotope imaging at the time of leukocyte labeling
or immediately after the completion of the radiolabeled leukocyte imaging. If Tc-99m
exametazime is used for the labeling of leukocytes, an interval of 48 to 72 hours is
necessary between the two imaging studies.
Bone marrow scintigraphy in combination with radiolabeled leukocyte scintigraphy
improves the accuracy of the diagnosis of osteomyelitis in patients in whom altered
bone marrow distribution is present. Sulfur colloid and radiolabeled leukocytes
physiologically localize to normal marrow. Only labeled leukocytes accumulate in sites of
infection/osteomyelitis, with sulfur colloid being discordantly absent9,31 (Figure 7). For
example, labeled leukocytes may accumulate around a total hip arthroplasty implant if
periprosthetic joint infection or aseptic loosening is present. Comparison with bone
marrow scintigraphy can confirm whether this labeled leukocyte activity is likely infection
(no correlating sulfur colloid activity) or hematopoietically active marrow from aseptic
loosening (correlating sulfur colloid activity).

Positron Emission Tomography
PET is a functional technique that creates 3D images by detecting annihilation radiation
emitted by positron-emitting radiopharmaceuticals. The paired photons produced allow for
accurate localization in three dimensions.
Circumferential views of the body are acquired via PET scanners, allowing for assessment of
the radiopharmaceutical distribution.

Positron Emission Tomography

AAOS | Molecular Imaging
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001020
16/29

PET can be combined with CT to improve anatomic localization of the
radiopharmaceutical agent. PET/CT scans obtain sequential PET and CT images that are
co-registered. The companion CT scan often is a low-dose non-contrast scan, whereas
some institutions perform diagnostic quality CT.9
Recently, PET in combination with MRI has become available. Advantages of MRI
compared with CT include superior soft-tissue contrast resolution, lack of radiation, and
additional information that may be gained from MRI.32 Clinical use of PET/MRI is limited
because of less accessibility of the technique, longer acquisition time, and increased
cost.
18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET
18F-fluoro-deoxyglucose (18F-FDG) is the most common radiopharmaceutical used for PET.
18F-FDG is an analog of glucose that is transported into cells by glucose transporters but does
not undergo additional metabolism.33.
Cellular uptake of 18F-FDG correlates with cellular metabolic rate.
18F-FDG PET in combination with CT or MRI provides detailed anatomic and metabolic
information. 18F-FDG PET/CT is commonly used in patients with various musculoskeletal
disorders.
Normal biodistribution includes brain, heart, red marrow, liver, kidneys, and urinary system.
18F-FDG PET is not specific; tumor and inflammatory tissues take up FDG, with generally higher
FDG uptake noted in tumors compared with inflammation.34-37
High serum glucose levels may reduce uptake of 18F-FDG in tumor, leading to false negatives
in patients with hyperglycemia.38-42
Fasting for at least 4 hours and avoidance of strenuous activity for at least 6 hours before 18F-
FDG injection minimizes radiopharmaceutical uptake in normal tissues. Serum glucose level
should be below 200 mg/dL.
18F-FDG is administered intravenously.
PET scans usually are acquired 60 minutes after radiopharmaceutical injection.
CT typically is performed before the PET scan and is used for attenuation correction and
anatomic localization.

MRI can be performed in a sequential manner (similar to PET/CT) or at the same time as PET.
MRI protocol includes an attenuation correction sequence followed by different diagnostic
sequences that vary according to clinical indication.
PET coverage usually is from the base of the skull to the mid-thigh. Additional coverage of the
head and extremities may be performed if appropriate.
18F-FDG is excreted by the kidneys. The urinary bladder is the organ that receives the highest
radiation dose.

18F-FDG PET/CT plays a key role in the evaluation of musculoskeletal tumors because of
its ability to provide unique information regarding metabolism (Figure 8).
Figure 8 Images of a 72-year-old-man with metastatic prostate cancer. A, Anterior whole-
body maximal intensity projection fluorine-18 sodium fluoride–labeled sodium fluoride
bone scans shows numerous foci of increased activity in the skeleton. Fused axial
positron emission tomography/CT scan of the pelvis (B) shows increased activity in
bilateral iliac bones and the sacrum, which corresponds with the sclerotic osseous
metastases observed on a CT scan of the pelvis (C). (Images courtesy of Juana Martinez,
New York, NY.)
Although 18F-FDG PET/CT typically is performed for evaluation of malignancy, many
benign bone lesions may be FDG-avid. For example, fibrous dysplasia, giant cell tumor,
and osteoid osteoma may demonstrate considerable activity on PET/CT.
18F-FDG PET/CT is especially useful for staging and evaluating treatment response and
recurrence.47-49

In the evaluation of musculoskeletal infections and inflammatory processes, 18F-FDG
PET/CT is associated with advantages compared with other imaging modalities, including
a shorter study duration and high-resolution images that provide functional and
anatomic information; however, lack of specificity and cost limit its use.50,51
18F-NaF Bone Scintigraphy
18F-NaF is a positron-emitting radiopharmaceutical with a half-life of 110 minutes.52
The advent of dual-modality PET/CT make 18F-NaF valuable in skeletal imaging, providing high-
resolution functional and anatomic images.53
The mechanism of bone uptake of 18F-NaF is similar to the Tc-99m labeled diphosphonates.
After chemisorption, 18F exchanges with hydroxyl ions on the surface of hydroxyapatite to
form fluoroapatite and subsequently is incorporated to the bone matrix.54
18F-NaF is administered intravenously.
Emission images of the axial skeleton can be obtained as soon as 30 to 45 minutes after
administration of the radiopharmaceutical. In patients with renal failure, a later start in the
acquisition might be necessary. To image the extremities, a waiting time of 90 to 120 minutes
after administration is recommended to obtain high-quality images.
The total radiation received by the patient is determined by the radiation emitted from the PET
radiopharmaceutical and the radiation dose from CT.10,13,55,56.
18F-NaF PET/CT primarily is used for the detection of osseous metastases in different types of
cancer.

18F-NaF Bone Scintigraphy
Several studies have reported increased sensitivity and specificity of 18F-NaF PET/CT
compared with Tc-99m–labeled diphosphonate bone scintigraphy in patients with
osseous metastases,.57-59 as well as the number of malignant lesions detected on
baseline. 18F-NaF PET/CT and standardized uptake value changes on follow-up scans
have been described to substantially correlate with overall survival in patients with
advanced prostate cancer.60 Despite its superior sensitivity and specificity, the clinical

dose received by the patients.
18F-NaF PET/CT also may be useful for several benign skeletal pathologies, such as back

osteonecrosis of the jaw.61-63
Novel Molecular Imaging Studies
Optical Imaging
Molecular technique based on the detection of photons of light using external cameras to
generate images
Fluorescence imaging uses molecules that absorb light and subsequently release light of a
longer wavelength. Near-infrared fluorophores are used in musculoskeletal molecular imaging.
Bioluminescence imaging uses the expression of luciferase protein (Figure 9).

Optical Imaging
Optical imaging is a promising technique for the evaluation of bone metabolism,
including bone turnover, damage, and repair. It also has shown value in evaluating
musculoskeletal infectious and inflammatory processes. Additional applications in
oncologic imaging also have been studied.64-66.
